Why does FEMA constantly try to reinvent the wheel? There is an existing method of providing nutritionally sound meals that self heat. The US military uses Meals Ready to Eat (MRE) for when our troops are away from mess facilities. The meals vary greatly with even vegetarian offerings. Each meal is sealed in a pouch that has a chemically activated pouch for heating. Each pouch contains other items needed in survival situations such as toilet paper & plastic utensils. Each pouch contains enough calories & protein to sustain a soldier for one day in a war zone with bullets whizzing overhead. There is the added benefit that the military is typically tapped to distribute supplies & meals during disasters. This provides a person who can teach how the MRE heatpacks work. They can also explain that spreading the food in the pouch over the entire day is how the MRE is designed.

These meals are packaged in cardboard cases designed for low altitude airdrops. The cases come on pallets designed for rapid higher altitude parachute drops. Does this not sound like exactly what is needed after a disaster? The military has stockpiles of these meals. They have to keep stockpiles. The shelf life on an MRE is measured in years, not months. An MRE lot is tested at its expiration date & recertified for several more years. The existing supply chain & manufacturing process can keep up with almost any demand. There is no need to issue new contracts.

My experience working in a pencil factory was just a leeeeeedle different.

I was given the lowliest task to sort the graphite lead rods that were to be fed into the huge German-made machine that applied them to the notched wood slats. My sorting tool was a wood box, open at the top, with two round metal bars mounted at an incline. I would take a handful of rods from their shipping box (the graphite was made elsehwere), and let them all roll from one end to the other. The broken pieces would fall away, and then I would take pack the unbroken pieces. When I had a few full boxes, I would wheel them over to the guy running the big machine.

I was of course ever trying to keep up with that machine which was ravenous. When it was running, it could use graphite faster than I could sort. The only way I was able to get ahead of it was when it broke down, which it mercifully did on a regular basis.

The place was caked in graphite dust, and noisy. Not quite Dickens, but not too far from it either. The day a woman lost three of her fingers working on a machine right next to me was memorable.

But oddly enough, I still love pencils and wouldn't trade them for a computer to draw with for anything in the world.

Like the classic Gem paper clip, the wooden pencil is a beautifully functional object whose design is essentially perfect: Every attempt to improve it produces an inferior pencil. Applause for General Pencil for simply continuing to do what it does best. And more applause for Christopher Payne and Sam Anderson for an excellent photo essay and article.

The only trouble with pencils, which is not the pencils' fault, is their tendency to not be at hand when you need one. For years I wasted time in my workshop looking for the pencil I'd laid down—somewhere—five minutes ago and now couldn't find. I worked to improve my mindfulness but it didn't help. Finally I hit on a solution based on the pencil's own nature: inexpensive and expendable. Once every few days I sharpen a half-dozen pencils and scatter them around the shop, ensuring there's always at least one somewhere in sight when I need it.

Somewhere, I'm sure, someone is working on an internet-enabled pencil that will broadcast its location to its owner's smartphone, but trust me: the classic pencil is just fine as it is.

I was a competitor back in the days when compulsory figures counted for 60% of the "score." Actually, back then we used an ordinal system that took into account how a skater placed with each judge. If you placed first with a judge, your ordinal from that judge was 1; if you placed second, your ordinal was 2 and so on. The skater with the lowest sum of ordinals was the winner. Ties were broken by adding up the actual technical and artistic scores (on the 6.0 scale).

Like many other commenters, I agree that the elimination of compulsory figures has changed the sport. Rarely does one see the edge control and smoothness fans became accustomed to. Well executed quads are a joy to behold, but skaters should not receive a higher score for attempting a quad and falling, than executing a comparable triple and landing it perfectly.

There is an underlying thread here that I think is the most interesting part of this article. It is the understanding that there is a human desire to have an answer for why things are the way they are. AND that our attachment to these ideas can be so strong that we will cling to them in the face of great contradictory evidence. It is a human weakness wether the human is a scientist or not. As a medical practitioner I can easily come up with examples where medicine was quite confident of something only to realize later that they were way off. Take any of a variety of women's gynecological illnesses. They were long ascribed to gender weakness and psychological failings. Now we know them as endometriosis, polyscystic ovarian syndrome, ovarian cysts etc.. But just 50-60 years ago we would have blamed the patient as flawed. Take ulcers. Just 30 yr ago we would blamed the patient as too stressed out and emotional. Now we know the vast majority of ulcers are caused by a bacteria. But when this was first discovered no one believed it. Now we have the same issues with obesity. The evidence is clear that there are multiple neuro-hormonal factors as well as genetic factors that have a profound effect on a persons ability to lose weight and sustain it. We have 70 yrs of evidence that "just diet" doesn't work yet many medical and most lay people cling to this prescription. Good science requires a genuinely open mind and the ability to let go of assumptions.

Statins are very effective in preventing recurrent events in those who have already suffered heart attack or stroke, according to the research. What does "effective" mean, really, when you are looking at 20-30% reduction in incidence when the side effect rate is at least 20-30%, and includes diabetes, cognitive disturbances, myalgias, liver damage, and many others. A serious side effect that hasn't been measured in clinical studies but has been reported commonly is that people who have lowered their cholesterol successfully with statins sometimes pay less attention to life style factors in disease such as exercise and diet. They are given a false sense of security from their lower cholesterol numbers and the big smile on their doctor's faces who read them these numbers. This discourages from doing what research and common sense would dictate are better interventions: getting more exercise and improving their diet to lose weight and improve overall health.

Statins are also touted as effective based on studies comparing them to placebo. However they have not been shown to be superior to other treatments for stroke and heart disease prevention. including fish oil, turmeric, garlic, co-enzyme Q10, Hawthorne, Gingko, dietary changes and exercise programs, especially when implemented concurrently.

"a well-educated society must understand its roots — the Delphic maxim “know thyself.” Well, "Know Thyself" has nothing to do with understanding oneself in a psychological sense, as we often (and wrongly!)interpret this saying to mean. Such an understanding was historically absent in Greek society at the time the temple of Apollo was built (on which the phrase is sculpted), and even for centuries later. The temple represented and maintained a religious and oracular tradition. People went there to ask the Oracle a question. The phrase, "Know Thyself," simply advised people to be aware of their place in their cosmos vis-à-vis the gods: they were puny, separated from the gods by immense distance. As Pindar sang in Pythian Ode VIII, "What are we?/The shadow of a dream, no more." I taught Western Civ for more than twenty years. This is a point I hope my students learned.

It was the summer of 1965 in Los Angeles, California. I had just lost my battle with calculus and physics in my college classes, dashing my dreams to enter a school of architecture. A few friends of mine had been in the California Air National Guard at Van Nuys, and suggested I join up, too; you know, take some time off from college to think about what I will do for a career.

I signed up and took the Oath in mid-September. That October, President Johnson gave his speech, "Why Vietnam?" Then the draft and lottery began. And on Dec. 6, I was flying to Lackland AFB for basic training.

While working on C-97 and C-130 cargo aircraft during my six years in the Guard, I quickly came to realize, as did Mr. Cronkite, that the Vietnam War was a lost cause. As the saying went, "You can kill the enemy but not the idea." I lost friends over there. A few were honored for their heroism and bravery. Some brought back their own stories of terror, jungle firefights with anunseen enemy. Some memorialized at the Vietnam War Memorial.

One colleague from my part-time job came home to a parade honoring him and others, at Camp Pendleton. He came to visit in his dress blues and looked every bit the hero. Then, he told us he was getting a medal for doing things that crushed his soul.

While on a trip to Maryland in 1988, I stopped in DC on a drizzly day to visit that Wall honoring our lost heroes from that dreadful war. I cried with total strangers. We hugged like brothers.

Roth remains at nearly 85, both erudite and carnal, a vaudevillian and a serious thinker.

I studied Roth in college when he was still considered an 'American Jewish' writer and learned an enormous amount from his work. Since then, his lifetime of original and moral thought put to paper with the comic rhythms (to me anyway) of the shtetl cements his place as a reader's treasure.

May he continue to greet each new day with surprise and delight for a long time to come.

I find almost all works of writers like Roth to be either boring or unreadable. I think they show off technical skills too much and choose too arcane theses. And I find the idea that fiction has "meaning" laughable.

But the word is a better place for their existence. We need such people. And once in a while I find a "high literary" book interesting.

Each to his own taste. I find equivalent creations in modern (classical) music and art absolutely enthralling. I think that is because while they may be, in their creator's verbal minds not to my taste, they have a life outside words.

We live in idiotic times, but then, as Americans, we always have. Roth, along with Saul Bellow, John Updike, Bernard Malamud, John Cheever, William Gaddis, Richard Yates, and a handful of others, compiled a rich chronicle of an America now dead and gone.

Their post-war America was by no means a perfect place (by no means!), but at least one in which it was possible to imagine a better time, and, in any case, the world they wrote about was beautifully imagined. Now, our literature, like our politics, is mostly cynical, ironic, and glib. Impossible to imagine any longer the great passion and artistry of Herzog or American Pastoral--that kind of commitment to craft and belief in the power of ideas is as antiquated as letter writing or conversation.

I anxiously await Bailey's biography (he wrote wonderfully of John Cheever) and Roth's long overdue Nobel Prize.

I'm 56. I've voted Democratic all my life. I loathe Trump and disagree with conventional conservatives on pretty much every issue. I've voted in every election since I turned 18, even off-year ballots that contained nothing but small local issues and even when I was in the midst of chemo.

I don't know where I'll go instead; certainly not to a party whose sole interest is redistributing wealth from workers to the rich despite their current thin veneer of populism. Maybe I'll become one of those people who feel so disenfranchised that they just give up. Maybe I'll vote third party. Who knows? We'll see what happens in the next two years.

Note that I said the Democrats should return to being the party of working *people* not just the party of what is commonly known as the working class. Most Americans work, are retired from working, or will someday work for a living. Work is our most unifying factor; most of us have to work for a living. Workers are the largest "identity group" in the nation. Democrats take note -- the party that can unite this group by representing their interests and by pointing out over and over again how Republican policies hurt those who work for a living will have a YUGE natural constituency.

The country is quite polarized--on a number of dimensions. Urban vs. rural. Working class vs. college educated "brainjob" holders. Religious vs. not.

One of the dimensions is not, however, Republican vs. Democrat--not in the traditional sense, anyway. As Edsall and his quoted note, there may well be a fundamental redefinition ongoing as to who supports which party.

It's tempting to think of things as populist vs. elite, but those categories have the habit of being rather fluid. Knowledge workers who might have considered themselves elite are about to be disrupted by automation and robots as well--it's already happening in design, architecture, law. It's hard to feel elite when you're a J.D. degree holder doing cold call selling or barista-ing.

Eventually, the party--existent or emerging--that addresses the fundamental shift in our economic lives, the changing nature of work as an identity as well as material living provider, will have a YUGE constituency. As others have noted, except for the MOST elite, almost all of us will have some form of working life. Those who address what is to be done when there is much less work to be done by people, and even most brain workers lose their premium (whether that involves shorter workweeks, guaranteed income, bigger safety nets/"entitlements") will garner many votes.

The question is, will such a movement emerge with enough energy before "the house divides", or climate change makes all these issues moot.

So the fault of our children’s dropping academic performance does not fall solely on the schools or on the parents – it also falls on the policy makers who built the existing system of public school funding and still disregard income inequality as a powerful force in determining whether or not our children will receive a high-quality education.

The national exit polls are wrong in another, even bigger way: they wildly oversample younger voters. Analyze the national sample of the 2016 presidential race and it implies the median age -- half younger, half older -- of voters was about 48 years old, meaning those who cast ballots were literally the same median age as the 40% of the electorate that DIDN'T vote at all. This is absurd on its face -- and rebutted by the July, 2017 Census survey showing a median age of closer to 52 for voters (and thus, about 44 for non-voters).
In midterms, in 2014 BOTH the exit polls (median age about 52) and the Census (about 54) are wrong. (How could the latter not be, when its self-report survey shows 92 million votes cast in 2014 -- when actual voting records show just 83 million?)
At Portland State work with complete voter files in 15 states reveal median voter ages closer to 57-58 in most 2014 midterm states; Arizona, whose eligible voter population is actually now slightly younger than the nation due to its growing Hispanic population, had a median age of 62 in 2014.
Those who've taken some solace in the "youth surge" of voting in recent elections, based on faulty Census poll data, have lulled themselves into semi-complacency and misplaced hope. My impression is that part what has lead many to think Ansari's conduct worthy of inclusion in #metoo (including some in this comments section) is that what we hear about these issues does not distinguish between ideas about what constitute best practices with those about what is required for acceptable, non-criminal behaviour.

For example, those of us under a certain age have grown up being told that affirmative verbal consent should always be obtained (the "yes means yes" standard). And we really should. Ansari should have. All of this likely wouldn't be happening if he had.

However, this is about best practices, not about the threshold of consensual sex vs rape or sexual assualt. If the latter were true, and affirmative verbal consent was required to make something not be rape, then millions of people would be guilty of having committed rape this very evening. The simple truth is that the vast majority of adults have had sex without prior verbal consent. People in long term relationships do so all the time. So it can't plausibly be the bar for legality, for avoiding widespread scorn and criminal punishment.

Instead, it's an attempt to get us in the habit of doings so. Because sometimes we think we've read all the subtle cues right and it turns out we didn't. Because we have a responsibility to help ensure that mistakes about consent stop happening.

We can say Ansari should have been more careful. But we can't punish him for doing what we all do.

Oddly, the author notes that "highly selective colleges" haven't jumped on the assessment-outcomes bandwagon. On its web page, UNC-Chapel Hill notes its students are "distinguished not only by their academic credentials, but also by their extraordinary creativity, perseverance, compassion, and humility." As a math professor at a college in California, I also see the trend that the writer identifies that's overwhelming higher education in America. Everyday I am bombarded with persistent appeals by textbook publishers to adopt their web-based curricula because "our unique digital solution" will simplify student assessments and quantify all learning outcomes. The goal is clear: Move everything online, let students take charge of their own learning (whatever that means), and you, the teacher, slowly disappear. Buzzwords like 'critical thinking', 'data-driven outcomes' and 'real-life problems' are liberally sprinkled in their glossy brochures and in the hefty, expensive tomes called textbooks. In this clash of jargon and analytics, single mothers, full-time employees and low-income students desperate to improve their lot with education are left holding a huge overdue bill but with diminishing returns every passing year. Teaching how to think and engage in protracted inquiry will not come from one-time assessment test per subject per semester/quarter but from teachers and students working together across months and even years to explore the deeper questions and solving problems worth solving, even if accompanied by a high risk of failure.
